Topic:Trains

Sat 4 Jul 2026 at 8:38am

Teralba and Broadmeadow in the NSW Hunter region have been identified as possible locations for the new factory. (ABC News: Declan Bowring)

The NSW premier has shortlisted two sites in the Hunter region for a factory to build a new fleet of trains.

The announcement, which was part of the government's pledge to revive manufacturing, was made at the NSW Labor state conference.

A protester was taken away by police after a Palestinian flag with a sticker listing "Labor values" was unfurled at the conference.

The New South Wales premier has pledged to revive train manufacturing in the state, earmarking two sites near Newcastle for a new factory.

Premier Chris Minns made the announcement in a speech at the NSW Labor Conference at Sydney Town Hall on Saturday morning.

He said the next set of trains would be manufactured "where the original fleet was built" in the state's Hunter region, at either Teralba or Broadmeadow.

"For generations, highly skilled Australian workers made our Tangaras, our red rattlers, our V Set, our S Set," Mr Minns told the party's rank-and-file.

"All until 2012, when the last train rolled off the line at Broadmeadow, after being outsourced to China, Spain and South Korea."

There was a commotion inside Sydney Town Hall ahead of the premier's speech. (ABC News)

In a separate statement, the government said $12 billion had been set aside for the project.

Ahead of his keynote speech, there was a commotion inside Sydney Town Hall as the premier made his entrance.

A Palestinian flag with a sticker listing "Labor values" was unfurled from a balcony, as Mr Minns greeted the party faithful.

Some delegates could be heard booing the protester, who was led away by police.

In a statement, NSW Police said two men, aged 49 and 60, were issued with a move-on direction, and inquiries into the incident were ongoing.

Minister for Transport John Graham said the plan would create hundreds of jobs.

"We are taking control of the process," he said.

Mr Graham said he "couldn't think of a better place" to revive the manufacturing of trains than near the original site where the Tangara was first built.

"This will mean hundreds of jobs for the Hunter, both in the construction, but also then in the long-term manufacturing for those jobs," he said.

"It's not just in those two areas, it's also the long-term logistics chains that this will build.

"We know we've got a number of those companies in the Hunter or in Western Sydney."

Mr Graham says the revival will create hundreds of jobs. (ABC News: Greg Bigelow)

The government had previously committed to start procuring the replacement of the ageing Tangara fleet by early 2027, with a "50 per cent local content target".

The $12 billion earmarked for the project would be spent over 15 years, but it was unclear where the funding would come from.

No money has been put aside for the project in this year's budget.
